output:
*Interview with Mme Odile Monnier, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Madame, I am sorry to keep you from your rest. I know what this night has been for you.

MME MONNIER: I have had no rest to keep, Inspector. Rosa told me, and I did not believe her. I am not sure I believe her now. I keep listening for him on the stairs.

MATTHEY: Take your time. When you are ready, tell me about the evening, from the beginning of dinner.

MME MONNIER: When the temple bell struck nine, my husband made us all take out our watches. He does it every year. He says that people who sit at his table should at least know what hour it is. Félix's watch showed twenty minutes to nine. Aurèle scolded him for it in front of everyone. He said Jules's watch was a disgrace to the family and that Félix ought to be ashamed to carry it. Félix laughed, as he does when he is frightened, and my husband did not let it go. He told the others what was wrong with their watches too, which is what he always did. I will not repeat all of it.

MATTHEY: And afterwards?

MME MONNIER: We went through to the salon. The doctor and I sat down to piquet. We have played piquet for thirty years, and I have never known Casimir to lose gracefully. When the temple struck ten I looked at the salon clock. It showed five minutes to ten.

MATTHEY: You played without a break?

MME MONNIER: Without a break. Not for a glass, not for anything, until he got up to fetch his cigars. He went out at twenty-eight minutes past ten by the salon clock.

MATTHEY: Did he say anything to you as he went?

MME MONNIER: He asked me to play for him. He always asks, and I always refuse at first, and then I do it. This time I sat down at the piano at once. I played Chopin, as I do when I do not know what else to do with my hands. I played until he came back, and I stopped when he came in.

MATTHEY: Do you recall the hour when he came back?

MME MONNIER: A moment after he came back, the hall clock struck eleven. That is all I can tell you about the hour, Inspector. I am not a clock.

MATTHEY: Of course. Tell me about your nephew. Is there anything about his affairs that you think I ought to know?

MME MONNIER: He owes money. I do not know how much, and I did not ask. Some of it is owed to Monsieur Girard. Félix has always borrowed from people who are not his friends, and he always believes the next loan will be the last.

MATTHEY: And at table, was there any disagreement?

MME MONNIER: Monsieur Girard wanted the repeater. He offered my husband a price for the rights to it, and Aurèle laughed at the price. They said things to each other that gentlemen do not say over the soup. It was almost a relief when the watches came out, because it gave us all something to do with our hands.

MATTHEY: Thank you. You have been very clear.

MME MONNIER: I have been exact, which is not the same thing, though people often confuse them. I am sorry if I have been cold. I will not cry in front of you, Inspector, if that is what you are waiting for. Aurèle would not have wanted it, and I have had thirty years of practice at not showing what I feel.
